concepts.def: To test the validity of psychiatric diagnosis: can sane people be reliably distinguished from the insane in hospital settings?
Eight pseudopatients reported a single symptom ('thud, empty, hollow') to gain admission to 12 hospitals across 5 US states.
All 8 were admitted; 7 diagnosed with schizophrenia, 1 with bipolar; average stay was 19 days; none detected as sane by staff.
Note-taking by pseudopatients was recorded as 'engaging in writing behaviour', interpreted through the schizophrenia label.
Hospital was warned to expect pseudopatients; staff identified 41 of 193 genuine patients as fake, though Rosenhan sent none.
Diagnostic categories lack validity; environment, not symptoms, drove categorisation; supported anti-psychiatry movement.

concepts.def: To investigate whether leading questions distort the recall of eyewitnesses to a car accident.
45 students watched seven film clips of car accidents and were asked how fast cars were going when they 'smashed/hit/contacted'.
Mean speed estimates: 'smashed' 40.8 mph, 'collided' 39.3, 'bumped' 38.1, 'hit' 34.0, 'contacted' 31.8 mph.
150 participants; one week later 32% who heard 'smashed' falsely recalled broken glass vs 14% who heard 'hit'.
Supports Bartlett: post-event information becomes integrated into memory rather than retrieved as a pure record.
Eyewitness testimony unreliable when leading questions are used; influenced UK PEACE interview model.

concepts.def: To test whether children imitate aggressive behaviour observed in an adult model, including across genders.
72 children aged 3-6 (36 boys, 36 girls) assigned to aggressive model, non-aggressive model or control; observed playing with Bobo doll.
Children in aggressive condition imitated physical and verbal aggression significantly more; boys more aggressive than girls.
Boys imitated male aggressive models more than female; girls showed weaker effect, supporting identification.
Bandura (1965) follow-up: children imitated less when model was punished, supporting role of consequences.
Founded social learning theory; criticised for ethical issues (potential lasting aggression) and lack of ecological validity (Bobo doll is for hitting).

concepts.def: To investigate how readily people conform to assigned social roles in a simulated prison environment.
24 male volunteers screened as 'mentally stable' randomly assigned to guard or prisoner roles in Stanford basement mock prison.
Guards became increasingly brutal; prisoners passive and depressed; study halted after 6 days of planned 14.
Anonymity (uniforms, mirrored glasses, numbers replacing names) reduced personal identity, raising aggression.
Participants identified with their roles so strongly that they internalised assigned behaviours; supports situational explanations.
Lack of informed consent, harm to prisoners (one had a breakdown); changed APA ethical guidelines; replicated by Reicher and Haslam (2006) with different results.
